newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: IMF SAYS TO ACCESS ZAMBIA FUNDING IN MAY. [Corrected 11:30 gmt]
newsitem.headline: IMF SAYS TO ACCESS ZAMBIA FUNDING IN MAY. [Corrected 11:30 gmt]

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Friday it would meet Zambian officials in May to review the country's economic performance under a three-year programme before making further financial commitments.
IMF country representative Elwaleed Taha said an IMF mission would visit Zambia early in May to begin dicussions on the second year of the Enhanced Structural Ajustment Facility(ESAF).

"The mission will come to Zambia in the first week of May to review the country's performance in the first year of ESAF and start negotiations for the second year. When the negotiations are completed, (financial) disbursements will be made," Taha said
In February, the IMF endorsed the country's economic performance under the first year of ESAF and released SDR 10 million (about $14 million) to the country.
Key achievements leading to the IMF endorsement included the reduction of inflation to the lowest annual level in eight years at 35 percent, and a 6.5 percent economic growth in 1996.
Other achievements included an increase in social sector spending at 34.5 percent, and progress in the privatisation of state-run enterprises.
Zambia regained its eligibility to use IMF financial resources in December 1995 after clearing arrears to the IMF of SDR 830.2 million.
The country was turned down for IMF funding in September 1987 after the accumulation of overdue financial obligations to the IMF.
Under an agreement reached last year the IMF endorsement in February means that Paris Club members will reschedule (corrects from "cut") Zambia's debt by 67 percent.

Zambia, whose total external debt stands at around $6.38 billion has a debt service-to-exports ratio of 20 percent. The government aims to reduce it to around 12 percent by the year 2000 by accessing further debt relief from the recently approved debt initiative for debt-burdened poor countries.

Zambia continues to enjoy the support of the IMF and World Bank, althouth Western bilateral donors cut aid to the country last year in protest against the manner in which general elections were organised in November.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the elections after the Frederick Chiluba government changed the electoral laws to ban some candidates from standing, including former president Kenneth Kaunda.
The government is trying to win back the support of bilateral donors whom it will meet on April 25 in London. A third of Zambia's $1.1 billion budget for 1997/98 is dependant on donor aid.
